sections.title: SAP Integrated Business Planning
sections.text:
2.1 SAP Integrated Business Planning
Architecture
In this section, we’ll cover the high-level solution architecture of SAP IBP.
Figure 2.1 illustrates the high-level solution architecture of SAP Integrated
Business Planning for sales and operations. On the right-hand side are the cross-
functional stakeholders that participate in the sales and operations planning
(S&OP) process, ranging from sales/marketing, demand planning, finance, and
supply chain to executives.
The primary way for participants to access, analyze, and modify the plans is via
the familiar Microsoft Excel interface. There is an Excel add-on that provides a
tab in the Excel ribbon to access various functions for planning. In addition,
participants also can access the web interface for embedded real-time analytics,
which are user-defined. The social collaboration aspect of the S&OP process is
enabled by SAP Jam or through SAP Build Work Zone (launched in 2018). All
shared content is available not only from the web interface but also from Excel.
To support the S&OP process cadence, SAP IBP supports process modeling a
process dashboard that is socially enabled to better engage participants. There
© 

75
is also an admin interface both for managing user roles and permissions and for
reconfiguring the SAP IBP planning data model and calculations.
At the core, all data is stored and calculated in the SAP HANA in-memory
database. This includes dimensions, attributes, key figures, calculations,
versions, user-defined scenarios, and simulations.
On the left side of Figure 2.1 are different data sources from which data can be
brought into SAP Integrated Business Planning for sales and operations securely
using SAP Cloud Integration for data services.
Figure 2.1 SAP IBP Architecture

76

sections.title: Planning Model
sections.text:
2.2 Planning Model
When a company implements SAP IBP, the first task is to define and configure
the planning model based on business requirements and populate it with data.
Then, based on the planning model, planners and analysts can create planning
views so they can work on the data using SAP Integrated Business Planning,
add-in for Microsoft Excel.
SAP IBP requires a model to describe the data structures that the plan operates
on. A planning model allows you to represent your business plan. It describes
the structure of your business plan in terms of data and calculations. It defines
how data is stored, calculated, and aggregated in the system. You can also think
of the planning model as a master plan that defines how the information is
stored and aggregated in the system.
From a technical perspective, a planning model is a collection of master data
and time series data that is organized in dimensions and enhanced with specific
calculations. SAP IBP lets you configure and customize your own planning
models to address your unique business requirements.
In this section, we’ll cover the various entities that comprise the planning model.
We’ll cover the key concepts about the entities and the relationships between
them. In Chapter 10, we’ll also go over how the entities in the planning model
are configured in SAP IBP using SAP Fiori apps.
All planning models in SAP IBP are based on the following entities:
Attributes
Master data types
Time profiles
Planning areas
Planning levels
Key figures
Versions and user-defined scenarios
In the following sections, we’ll discuss each of these entities, followed by
coverage of multilanguage support for modeling objects, which is applicable for
some planning model entities.
© 

77

sections.title: Attributes
sections.text:
2.2.1 Attributes
Attributes are the fundamental elements that carry information about a
business entity. A logical grouping of attributes is used to model master data
types, which represent supply chain or business entities. Attributes describe the
characteristics of master data types; for example, a product entity is represented
by a unique product identifier (also known as product number), description,
product family, brand, category, and so on. Therefore, the first step in the design
phase of a project is to identify all relevant attributes.
Based on the property of the attribute, it can be defined as either numeric or
nonnumeric. The following data types are supported for attributes in SAP IBP:
String or varchar
This data type is the most widely used and represents character information
such as product description, product family, customer name, and so on.
Decimal
The decimal data type is used to maintain numerical information that
typically remains the same across the planning horizon. It’s also used for
modeling attributes as key figures. The information generally considered for
decimal attributes includes costs, exchange rates, unit of measure, capacity
supply, capacity consumption rates, components, and so on.
Integer
The integer data type is used to represent information such as lead time,
periods of coverage, or demand category, or system settings such as lot-size
policy.
Timestamp
Date or time information is represented using timestamp attributes. Phase-in
and phase-out date and product availability date are examples of timestamp
attributes.
To support the planning calendar function of SAP IBP, special attribute types are
available with fixed properties such as calendar attribute and time zone
attribute. You can define transportation and production calendars which
account for nonworking days to ensure that the correct quantity of goods is
manufactured and delivered on time.

78

sections.title: Master Data Types
sections.text:
2.2.2 Master Data Types
Master data contains main categories of information related to the supply chain
network entities. Master data is used to segment and organize planning
information. For example, customer, location, product, and resource are some of
the main or simple data categories within the data model. You can also combine
the main data categories to create compound data categories—for example, if
you want to understand the sales history based on a combination of product,
customer, and shipping location.
Master data types generally have many attributes or supporting data. Attributes
are characteristics of master data types that can be numeric or nonnumeric. For
example, an attribute of the location master data type could be the country,
location type, or region.
SAP IBP supports the following master data types:
Simple master data types
These represent foundational business objects or entities such as product,
customer, location, and resource.
Compound master data types
These are used to represent characteristics of combinations made of two or
more simple master data types. For example, if you have a business
requirement to analyze data by a combination of product and customer
characteristics, then you need to create customer-product compound master
data, made of the primary keys of two simple master data types: customer
and product. The compound master data type can have attributes such as
market segment.
Reference master data types
A reference master data type refers to a simple or compound master data type
so that you don’t have to upload the same data more than once. For example,
you can create the locationfr (location from) reference master data type that
uses the location master data type as a reference. You can’t load data into a
reference master data type.
Virtual master data types
Virtual master data types define joins between two or more master data types
that otherwise have no connection to each other. The join conditions you
define between these referenced master data types determine the set of data
the virtual master data type uses. You can only use simple and compound
© 

79
master data types to define virtual master data. In addition, you can’t load
data into a virtual master data type.
External master data types
External master data types let you manage master data integrated from an
external database into predefined static tables in SAP IBP. The prerequisite to
define external master data is to integrate the data from the external database
in a predefined format into SAP IBP. When you set up your planning model,
you define an external master data type referring to a predefined table that
contains the content. You can’t manually load data into external master data
types. The data is loaded into them from an external database via periodic-
based integration.

sections.title: Time Profiles
sections.text:
2.2.3 Time Profiles
A time profile is the time component of the dimensions; it defines the various
time levels (days, weeks, months, quarters, years) of time buckets, each with a
unique number, in which data can be managed. Each level is made up of
periods, which are identified by a number, and each has a start and end of the
time period. In SAP IBP, the time profile levels are customizable, which allows for
the flexibility to organize data.
To aggregate and disaggregate on time dimensions, hierarchies on different time
levels need to be defined. Figure 2.2 shows an example of a time hierarchy. In
this example, the time profile levels have multiple parents, and there also can be
time profile levels without a parent level.
Figure 2.2 Time Profile Levels Hierarchy

80

sections.title: Planning Areas
sections.text:
2.2.4 Planning Areas
A planning area describes the structure of an SAP Integrated Business Planning
for sales and operations plan and is the foundation of the planning model. It’s a
planning model entity defined by a set of other planning model elements that
includes attributes, master data, time profiles, planning levels, key figures, and
versions.
Figure 2.3 illustrates the relationship between the planning area entity and other
planning entities.
Figure 2.3 Planning Area Entities
The planning areas may contain many plan data sets: one actual or baseline
data set and many version data sets for storing alternate plans for what-if
analysis. An organization may have multiple planning areas to enable the S&OP
process in different business units.

sections.title: Planning Levels
sections.text:
2.2.5 Planning Levels
It’s very important in the SAP IBP or S&OP process to slice, dice, and analyze
data by different dimensions. A planning level is based on any set of attributes
that is a function of dimensions (e.g., product, customer, or location).
A planning level entity lets you analyze planning data at an aggregation level,
which is different from the storage or calculation level. Key figures in SAP IBP are
calculated or stored at specific planning levels.
Planning levels have two types of attributes:
Root attributes
Root attributes form the keys to independently identify the key figure values.
Typically, root attributes are also the keys of the master data, but this isn’t
always the case.
© 

81
Nonroot attributes
Nonroot attributes can be thought of as supporting data. They are
characteristics (or sometimes hierarchies) that help to aggregate the key
figure values.
Additionally, in key figure configuration, the planning level can be used as a base
planning level, which specifies the lowest level at which the value of the key
figure is defined. For the planning level to be used as a base planning level in a
key figure configuration, certain rules with regards to use of the base planning
level and its assignment to key figures must be fulfilled.
A stored planning level is defined when a planning level is used as the base
planning level of at least one stored key figure. This planning level can’t have the
time dimension as the root attribute.
For example, if the consensus demand stored key figure is defined and stored at
the week-product-customer planning level, then this key figure can be
aggregated by other nonroot attributes of the time dimension (e.g., month,
quarter, or year), of the product dimension (e.g., product family, or brand), and
of the customer dimension (e.g., customer region or key customer).
A planning area typically includes key figures of multiple planning levels, and
these can be linked with calculations, often resulting in key figures at additional
planning levels.

sections.title: Key Figures
sections.text:
2.2.6 Key Figures
Key figures are measures that hold transaction data. They are a series of
numbers over time, and each number corresponds to a time period value. Key
figures are associated with a key (of the planning level), which is a combination
of attributes from one or more master data objects. Some examples of key
figures include sales forecasts, marketing forecasts, consensus demand plans,
projected inventories, capacity plans, or actual data such as sales orders and
order history.
SAP IBP has the following types of key figures:
Stored
Data is stored in this type of key figure at the base planning level. The base
planning level is the lowest, most granular (key) planning level at which the

82
value of that key figure is defined. Data in a stored key figure is either edited
or imported directly.
Calculated
Values in this type of key figure are always calculated based on a formula.
Formulas are user-defined—for example, Revenue = (Quantity × Price). This
type of key figure isn’t editable.
Alert
These are key figures with user-defined criteria that monitor and manage
execution of business plans. They can only have values of 0 or 1, meaning that
the alert itself is either true or false—for example, you can have it alert you if
(Target revenue – Consensus revenue) ÷ Consensus revenue > 10%.
Snapshot
Snapshots are used to check how the key figure has evolved over time.
Selected key figures can be snapshotted at regular intervals by setting up an
application job. The values captured in this way are stored in a snapshot key
figure. The values of snapshot key figures are displayed in planning view,
which allows the creation of a time-lapse view of the data. For example, you
can snapshot consensus demand key figure at a particular time of the month
per the planning cycle of your business and further use it for forecast error
calculations.

sections.title: Versions and User-Defined Scenarios
sections.text:
2.2.7 Versions and User-Defined Scenarios
Versions let you maintain alternate global plans. Planning areas can contain
many plan data sets: one baseline data set and alternate plan data sets. Versions
let you perform what-if analysis on different versions of data. There are two
types of versions:
Versions that share master data with a base version
Versions that have their own master data (also called version-specific master
data)
The type of version is defined in configuration, and it can’t be changed once the
planning area is activated. A planning area can have a combination of the two
types of versions.
In addition to versions, you can also create user-defined scenarios. As the name
suggests, these are created by business users to enable what-if/simulation
© 

83
analysis. These are private to a user by default but can be shared with other
business users for collaborative decision-making. User-defined scenarios use
delta logic, as opposed to versions, which are complete copies. Delta changes in
key figure values are on top of versions and can be published back to versions.
Figure 2.4 illustrates the relationship between versions and user-defined
scenarios.
Figure 2.4 Versions and User-Defined Scenarios
The versions are alternate plans. The figure shows that the planning area has
three versions: base, optimistic, and pessimistic. The optimistic version shares
master data with the base version, whereas the pessimistic version has its own
master data. The master data and key figure data can be copied from other
versions.
The user-defined scenarios are on top of the versions and can be based on one
or more versions. Only the delta transaction data is stored in the user-defined
scenarios. The data is visible via shine-through logic from the underlying
versions.

sections.title: Multilanguage Support for Modeling Objects
sections.text:
2.2.8 Multilanguage Support for Modeling Objects
Multilanguage support helps in handling the supported modeling objects in
multiple languages. Once this multilanguage support is set up, it displays the
supported modeling object properties in logon language of the SAP IBP
applications where all these translations are available.
Multilanguage settings are system specific, so you need to specify them for each
of your systems. The multilanguage support works for key figures (name and
description), attributes (name and description), and planning area (description).

84

sections.title: Navigating the Planning Model
sections.text:
2.3 Navigating the Planning Model
The ability to navigate through SAP IBP is one of the most important aspects
getting the best out of SAP IBP. In this section, we’ll walk through how various
participants, including business users, administrators, and configuration
experts, can access various UIs offered by SAP IBP (e.g., Excel, web-based SAP
Fiori apps, and social collaboration) to accomplish their business objectives.
Once the planning model as described in the previous section is configured,
activated, and loaded with master data and transaction data, the planning
process can start.

sections.title: Excel User Interface
sections.text:
2.3.1 Excel User Interface
The primary way for participants to access, analyze, modify, and simulate plans
is via the Excel interface. SAP Integrated Business Planning, add-in for Microsoft
Excel, provides a tab in the Excel ribbon for viewing and changing planning
information in Microsoft Excel. The add-in supports localized date and number
formats, and it selects your local date and number format automatically.
The add-in also provides advanced planning functions such as supply planning
algorithms, statistical forecasting models, and disaggregation and copy planning
operator functions, depending on the applications your company has licensed
and the business role you’re assigned.
Before business users can use the add-in, it needs to be installed. The
installation can be done manually, or the add-in can be installed via silent
installation by your company’s SAP IBP administrator.
Before you can start working with your data in Excel, you need to establish a
secure connection between Excel and SAP IBP. A connection will establish access
to a planning area in a specific system and enable the different buttons in the
IBP tab in the Excel ribbon.
Figure 2.5 SAP IBP Tab in Excel
Now, let’s go over the different groups in the SAP IBP tab (see Figure 2.5) and
their functions:
© 

85
Connection
Allows you to log on to an SAP IBP planning area in the system or log off from
the SAP IBP planning area. The default method of logging on is via a SAML-
based connection. When you log on to the system using this connection,
you’re redirected to an identity provider and asked to submit your
credentials. Figure 2.6 illustrates the connection elements that need to be
populated in the connection manager.
Figure 2.6 SAP IBP Connection Manager
When logging off, you can choose to log off from the planning area; if you
choose this option, you log off from the SAP IBP system, which means that the
Remember Me setting is deleted, along with your credentials for the identity
provider used by your company. Alternately, you can choose to disconnect
from the SAP IBP system.
Planning View
Planning views let you perform planning tasks in SAP IBP. A planning view is a
user-defined report that allows for viewing, editing, and sharing information
directly from/into the SAP IBP system. The Planning View group in the SAP
IBP tab allows you to create and customize planning views. The created
planning views can be stored as favorites. The Planning View group also
provides quick access to edit the planning views and the filters. An Excel
workbook can contain multiple planning views in each sheet.
Data Input
Once you have the planning views created, the Data Input group in the SAP

86
IBP tab lets you edit the data, run simulations, and save the data per your
business needs. The Simulate dropdown lets you perform what-if analysis. It
also enables you to simulate advanced planning functions such as time-series
supply planning algorithms or inventory optimization functions.
The Refresh button lets you discard any unsaved changes you’ve made in
simulation mode or otherwise and refreshes the latest data from the
persistent or database layer.
Alerts
The Dashboard option shows the number of exceptions for the alerts added
in your favorite planning view.
Master Data
The Master Data group in the SAP IBP tab lets you make minor ad hoc
changes to the master data in your system, which is helpful for what-
if/scenario planning. It isn’t designed to replace data integration. It also
allows you to create planning objects. There are two options to manage
master data from the master data group:
Single: Lets you add, copy, edit, or delete single master data records (see
Figure 2.7).
Mass: The mass maintenance function lets you download master data
records from a master data type to a Microsoft Excel worksheet to view or
edit the data (see Figure 2.8). If your planning model supports version-
dependent master data, the system allows you to specify the version. The
mass maintenance function also lets you create new planning object
combinations. You can save the Excel workbook as a favorite.
© 

87
Figure 2.7 Manage Single Master Data
Figure 2.8 Manage Mass Master Data
Scenarios
As we discussed earlier, user-defined scenarios are created by business users
to enable what-if/simulation analysis. The Scenarios group in the SAP IBP tab

88
lets you create and manage user-defined scenarios. Figure 2.9 shows the
creation screen for user-defined scenarios. Here, you can create a new
scenario and share it with selected users or user groups.
Figure 2.9 Create User-Defined Scenario
Figure 2.10 shows the Manage Scenarios screen. From this screen, you can
promote a user-defined scenario to the underlying version; reset the scenario,
which basically initializes it; delete the scenario; or duplicate or copy an
existing scenario.
Figure 2.10 Manage User-Defined Scenarios
Versions
The Versions group in the SAP IBP tab lets you manage the transfer of master
data and transaction data between versions. The base version comes
standard with the system; you’ll need to configure any additional versions
© 

89
and activate them. The master data can only be copied between versions if a
version has its own master data.
Advanced
From the Advanced group in the SAP IBP tab, you can run advanced planning
functions such as time-series supply planning algorithms, inventory
optimizations, and statistical forecasting functions in background mode.
Tasks
From the Tasks group, you can directly display tasks that you’ve set up in the
Process Modeling app from SAP Fiori and change their status to Completed.
When you click the Tasks button, it opens the Processes and Tasks dialog,
containing a list of your open tasks (see Figure 2.11). You can choose to group
your tasks based on Process, Priority, or Due Date.
Figure 2.11 Task Management
Web Client
From here, you can open the Collaboration app or navigate to the web
interface homepage.
Template Admin
A template is a stored planning view that allows you to create planning views
based on your planning tasks and role. When you create a planning view

90
based on a template, the default settings such as time periods, key figures,
and planning levels are inherited. The new planning view is based on the
template’s Excel workbook, so any items stored in the workbook itself, such
as formatting, charts, or EPM local members, are also part of the new
planning view. However, the system doesn’t save the filter criteria as a
template setting.
Users with appropriate permissions can add new templates and edit or delete
existing templates.

sections.title: Web-Based SAP Fiori Applications
sections.text:
2.3.2 Web-Based SAP Fiori Applications
In addition to the Excel interface, SAP IBP offers a web UI for web-based SAP
Fiori apps. SAP Fiori apps are supported for desktop and tablets. The SAP Fiori
launchpad is the access point for all web-based applications for SAP IBP.
We’ll start off this section by introducing you to the SAP Fiori launchpad: how to
navigate it, how to find the apps you need, and how to personalize it. Then, we’ll
review some SAP Fiori apps to understand how you can use these web
applications in your S&OP process, different features offered by each app, and
the flexibility you have to model different apps based on your business needs.
We’ll review the Planner Workspaces app to understand how it can be used to
set up alerts, planning views, and charts to manage the plan. Then, we’ll discuss
web-based planning to understand how it’s leveraged for collaboration with
customers and suppliers. Finally, we’ll discuss how the Intelligent Visibility app
provides visibility into your entire supply chain and how you can manage plans
by exceptions.
SAP Fiori Launchpad
SAP Fiori apps are displayed as tiles, and you can launch any app by clicking the
corresponding tile from the launchpad. Figure 2.12 shows the SAP Fiori
launchpad screen for SAP IBP.
The tiles displayed on your launchpad are arranged into groups, with the group
title displayed above each group. The tiles can be rearranged within the group
by dragging and dropping them. You can’t add tiles or remove tiles from the tile
group.
© 

91
The set of tiles visible to you in the launchpad is determined by the business
catalogs assigned to the business roles that your business user is assigned to.
The business catalogs and the corresponding tile groups are delivered as part of
SAP IBP. A few examples of SAP Fiori groups and tiles available based on the
roles assigned are Demand Planner, Inventory Planner, General
Maintenance, and Model Configuration. The language for the text is
determined by the preferred language defined in your web browser. You can
change the language in the SAP Fiori launchpad by changing the default
language of your web browser.
When you log in, the first SAP Fiori group you’ll see is called My Home, which
you can customize to include your most commonly used functions. The SAP Fiori
launchpad also provides a quick way to edit your homepage, find SAP Fiori apps,
edit settings, and provide feedback by clicking on the user or person icon.
Figure 2.12 SAP Fiori Launchpad for SAP IBP
Figure 2.13 illustrates how to access the edit homepage, find SAP Fiori apps, edit
settings, and provide feedback. The left panel becomes available after clicking
the user or person icon at the top-right corner.

92
Figure 2.13 SAP Fiori Launchpad: Edit
In the left-hand panel, you can click the App Finder icon to find SAP Fiori apps.
Figure 2.14 illustrates the App Finder page. It lists the available apps on the left
and shows the existing SAP Fiori groups to which you can add apps on the right.
Figure 2.14 App Finder Page
You can also edit your settings by clicking the Settings icon. Figure 2.15 shows
the settings that can be changed.
© 

93
Figure 2.15 Edit Settings
In addition, you can also quickly edit your homepage by clicking the Edit
Homepage icon. This lets you add SAP Fiori apps to existing SAP Fiori groups,
including My Home; create new SAP Fiori groups; and rearrange the order of SAP
Fiori groups. Figure 2.16 shows the screen from which you can edit the
homepage.
Figure 2.16 Edit Homepage Screen

94
Planner Workspaces
Planner workspaces use the web UI to provide users a place to manage plans by
creating various alerts, planning views, and charts. You can set up the UI
specifically for your business scenario and manage the plan and exceptions.
Alerts, planning views, and charts are the three main components of a planner
workspace. You can flexibly organize them either for the same scenario or
different scenarios per your preference. These workspace components get
updated simultaneously; for example, if you set up the planning view with the
key figures you’ve used in the alerts component, any change in the planning
view will update the alerts simultaneously without having to switch between
different apps.
You can set up planner workspaces using the edit and copy functions, simple
dragging and dropping components, flexibly adjusting the column layouts, and
moving around the components. Appearance settings of the planner workspaces
can be modified to make them public and can be shared with other planners or
planner groups.
Once the planner workspaces are set up per your requirements, you can use
them for reviewing the highlighted key figures with alerts. You can modify the
plan in different scenarios to simulate the effect of changes. Once you’re
satisfied with the results of simulations, you can save the plan. These scenarios
can be shared with other planners or planner groups. Various other features
such as scheduling the applications jobs, fixing/unfixing the key figure values,
and adding keywords to planning notes can be performed within the planner
workspaces.
Figure 2.17 shows an example of a planner workspace set up by a supply
planner.
© 

95
Figure 2.17 Planner Workspace
Web-Based Planning for Customers and Suppliers
You can use the Web-Based Planning app for collaboration with your internal
business partners as well as external business partners such as customers and
vendors. You can use this app to create planning views per business needs with
the specific key figures. Key figure data can be changed in various scenarios for
simulation. After you’re satisfied with the results of simulations, you can save
the key figure data. You can also share planning views and/or scenarios in this
app with other planners or planner groups. Various other features such as
fixing/unfixing of the key figure values, management of notes and assigning
reasons codes can be leveraged for better collaboration.
For collaboration with customers, you can provide direct access to your SAP IBP
system to customers for specifically identified key figure data relevant for
collaboration. You can share the planning views with customers with key figure
data such as forecasted demand, capacity, and availability. Customers can then
directly enter their forecast in an easy-to-use Excel-like planning view key figures
via a web application. Figure 2.18 shows an example of a planning view setup in
the Web-Based Planning app for collaboration with customer ABC. It shows the
customer forecast key figure in which the customer can easily enter the data.
Customer receipts are the current receipts you’ve planned. You can create and
manage scenario for simulations. Planning view settings enable you to have
better control of the information you can share by selecting specific key figures
and applying specific filters.

96
Figure 2.18 Web-Based Planning: Customer Planning View
Figure 2.19 Web-Based Planning: Supplier Planning View
Similarly, for collaboration with suppliers, you can set up planning views with
specific key figures that are relevant from a supplier point of view; for example,
the vendor can have real-time visibility of your requirements in terms of the
most up-to-date demand forecast with which the supplier can make decisions
and supply-side commitments. Figure 2.19 shows an example planning view
setup in the Web-Based Planning app for collaboration with a supplier.
Intelligent Visibility
The Intelligent Visibility app provides you with visibility of your entire supply
chain network on a geographic map and enables you to manage exceptions. You
can navigate to your custom alerts and charts to understand the exact issue in
the supply chain. You can leverage customers by location, supply chain network,
or key figure layers on a geographic map. You can also set up the intelligent
visibility profile per your requirements, which you can apply in your Intelligent
Visibility app. Other planners also can share intelligent visibility profiles with
you. The Intelligent Visibility and Intelligent Visibility Profiles apps can be
accessed under the Intelligent Visibility application group (see Figure 2.20).
© 

97
Figure 2.20 Intelligent Visibility App and Intelligent Visibility Profiles App
As a first step, you create an intelligent visibility profile. Profiles are used to
customize the way you want to view data in the Intelligent Visibility app. Various
settings are performed, such as key figures you want to use, key figure value
formats, color, and the sequence in which you want to apply data filters. You
need to add charts to the profile. You define the layout of the charts per your
requirements and apply filters for your relevant data. The charts will apply these
filters when the profile is applied and location details are shown, according to
the chosen applied filters. You can share this profile with other team members
or groups. Figure 2.21 shows an example of an intelligent visibility profile.
Figure 2.21 Intelligent Visibility Profile
To review the supply chain network in the Intelligent Visibility app, you need to
select the data layers such as Customer, Location, Alerts, Supply Chain
Network, or Key Figures. You can apply filters to select the data set you want to
view in the app. You can then apply the intelligent visibility profile to apply all
the settings to your data set, such as value format, color, and so on. Once the

98
data is selected and the profile applied, you can navigate to Alerts, which you
can see on the map, and drill down to customers, locations, and so on. You can
also navigate to Charts to analyze the issues further. Figure 2.22 shows an
example of the Intelligent Visibility app.
Figure 2.22 Intelligent Visibility App: Data Layers

sections.title: Social Collaboration
sections.text:
2.3.3 Social Collaboration
The social collaboration aspect of the S&OP process is enabled by two different
tools, SAP Build Work Zone and SAP Jam. Based on your SAP IBP system license,
you’ll have access to one of these tools. As you plan and respond, you might
want to share with and get input from your colleagues. The integration of SAP
IBP with SAP Build Work Zone and SAP Jam lets you collaborate with other
members of your team and track your processes and process-related tasks. SAP
Build Work Zone is a newer tool for collaboration and offers similar
functionalities as SAP Jam.
You create collaboration groups in both the tools for specific topics and areas in
your S&OP. You can add relevant members to the group who can then
collaborate, share information with the group (e.g., Demand Review and Supply
Review collaboration groups), and assign relevant members to the group.
Both SAP Build Work Zone and SAP Jam can be accessed from the launchpad
using the Collaboration app (see Figure 2.23) when a direct link to these tools is
available.
© 

99
Figure 2.23 Collaboration App
In the following sections, you’ll learn more about how these tools are used for
social collaboration in SAP IBP for effectively managing S&OP processes within
the organization.
SAP Build Work Zone
The SAP Build Work Zone page (see Figure 2.24) is very user friendly and is
divided into various customizable sections such as the header bar, as well as the
Home, My Workspace, Applications, Workspace, and Tools tabs. Each section
has multiple features and is customizable based on access provided by your
administrator.
You use the header bar to set up user profiles, find apps, display notifications,
access the inbox, and perform general searches. The Home page is the page
launched when you access SAP Build Work Zone. Most of the content is set up by
your company administrator, but you can set up your My Workspace overview
section to add apps and tools you access frequently for managing S&OP
processes.
My Workspace is a personal workspace divided into Workspace, Content, and
Trash sections where you can add your favorite content, tools, and apps (see
Figure 2.25).

100
Figure 2.24 The SAP Build Work Zone Page
Figure 2.25 Workspace Set Up by a Planner
The Applications section enables you to add other business applications for
which you have permission to access.
Workspace is the most important section where you collaborate with other
team members. Typically, multiple collaboration groups are created within the
organization to manage S&OP processes; for example, the Demand Review
collaboration group will have demand planners who are managing demand
© 

101
review. Once you’re added to a collaboration group, you can start collaborating
with members of the group. You can also set up a workspace and add members
to it. While creating a workspace, you can use various features such as setting up
the workspace as public, private, or external; maintaining the collaboration level
as read-only, limited, or full; selecting the visibility policy, and so on. You can
add content such as business applications, decision-making tools, planning
tools, cards, widgets, feeds, forums and so on based on what you need to
manage your S&OP process and the content that is relevant for collaboration
(see Figure 2.26).
Figure 2.26 Typical Workspaces for S&OP Collaboration
Using the Tools section, you can access tools such as Tasks, Recommendations,
Bookmarks, Calendar, Knowledge Base, and Business Records.
SAP Build Work Zone can be seamlessly integrated with Google Drive, Microsoft
SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, SAP SuccessFactors Learning, and the SAP
SuccessFactors platform. The integration with these applications needs to be
enabled. Once they are enabled, you can easily switch to the applications from
SAP Build Work Zone.

102
SAP Jam
The SAP Jam homepage (see Figure 2.27) lets you view your home feed, enter
status updates, and start a discussion with colleagues; it also provides many
other tools that make collaboration easier.
Figure 2.27 SAP Jam Homepage
With SAP Jam Collaboration, you can perform the following actions:
You can view and create tasks and assign the tasks to SAP Jam groups for
each process step from the Manage Process Templates app. Figure 2.28 shows
a list of tasks assigned to the process steps from the process template. When a
process instance is created, tasks are also created for each user assigned to
the SAP Jam group (see Figure 2.29) in that process step.
You can share business data and other information with members of an SAP
Jam group by using the Share in SAP Jam button in the apps in which it’s
available. For example, you can share an application job template, a custom
alert, an analytics chart, a dashboard, or information about a transportation
lane with members of a specific SAP Jam group. Figure 2.30 shows how an
analytics chart can be shared by clicking the Share icon at the bottom-right
corner and choosing Share on SAP Jam.
You can also share business data such as an analytic chart with comments
directly to SAP Jam group members (see Figure 2.31).

sections.title: Summary
sections.text:
2.4 Summary
In this chapter, we covered the key concepts that enable planning processes
across SAP IBP applications. We focused on the building blocks used to
construct the planning models, such as attributes, time profiles, planning areas,
planning levels, key figures, and versions. We reviewed the features of a few
apps such as planner workspaces, web-based planning for customers and
suppliers, and intelligent visibility. Finally, we went over the various ways in
which super users or planners can interact with or navigate through the
planning model and applications depending on their roles. These options
include the web application interface via SAP Fiori apps, Excel planning views,
SAP Jam, and the SAP Build Work Zone collaboration platforms.
